claim: Ionotropic neurotransmitter receptors at postsynapses mediate fast synaptic transmission upon binding of the neurotransmitter.
source: Ionotropic neurotransmitter receptors at postsynapses mediate fast synaptic transmission upon binding of the neurotransmitter.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about how ionotropic receptors function.

claim: Post- and trans-synaptic mechanisms through cytosolic, membrane, and secreted proteins have been proposed to localize neurotransmitter receptors at postsynapses.
source: Post- and trans-synaptic mechanisms through cytosolic, membrane, and secreted proteins have been proposed to localize neurotransmitter receptors at postsynapses.
evidence: This statement references prior proposals in the literature about receptor localization mechanisms.

claim: It remains unknown which mechanism is crucial to maintain neurotransmitter receptors at postsynapses.
source: However, it remains unknown which mechanism is crucial to maintain neurotransmitter receptors at postsynapses.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in knowledge that the study addresses.

claim: Excitatory AMPA receptors remain at the postsynaptic density upon ablation of excitatory presynaptic terminals.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that excitatory AMPA receptors remain at the postsynaptic density upon ablation of excitatory presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2 and 3.

claim: Inhibitory GABAA receptors required inhibitory presynaptic terminals for their postsynaptic localization.
source: In contrast, inhibitory GABAA receptors required inhibitory presynaptic terminals for their postsynaptic localization.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Ectopic expression at excitatory presynapses of neurexin-3 alpha can recruit GABAA receptors to contacted postsynaptic sites.
source: Consistent with this finding, ectopic expression at excitatory presynapses of neurexin-3 alpha, a putative trans-synaptic interactor with the native GABAA receptor complex, could recruit GABAA receptors to contacted postsynaptic sites.
evidence: This finding is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic receptors utilize distinct mechanisms for their maintenance in the mature mammalian brain.
source: These results establish distinct mechanisms for the maintenance of excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic receptors in the mature mammalian brain.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Fast excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmissions in the mature brain are mostly mediated by ionotropic AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) and GABAA receptors (GABAARs), respectively.
source: Fast excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmissions in the mature brain are mostly mediated by ionotropic AMPA-type glutamate receptors (AMPARs) and GABAA receptors (GABAARs), respectively.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about neurotransmission.

claim: The maintenance of AMPARs and GABAARs at the corresponding postsynapse involves various components, including postsynaptic cytosolic scaffolding proteins and trans-synaptic components, such as membrane and secreted proteins.
source: The maintenance of these receptors at the corresponding postsynapse involves various components, including postsynaptic cytosolic scaffolding proteins and trans-synaptic components, such as membrane and secreted proteins (Barrera-Ocampo and Chater, 2013; Gerrow and El-Husseini, 2007; Luscher et al., 2011; Martenson and Tomita, 2015; Moss and Smart, 2001).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: It is less clear which of these mechanisms is crucial for maintaining neurotransmitter receptors at postsynapses in vivo.
source: However, it is less clear which of these mechanisms is crucial for maintaining neurotransmitter receptors at postsynapses in vivo.
evidence: This identifies the knowledge gap addressed by the study.

claim: Acetylcholine receptors remain at synapses of the neuromuscular junction after denervation.
source: Acetylcholine receptors remain at synapses of the neuromuscular junction after denervation, highlighting the importance of the postsynaptic machinery for its maintenance at synapses (Hartzell and Fambrough, 1972).
evidence: This is a finding from prior literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: Denervation of specific neurons is not feasible in the brain.
source: As denervation of specific neurons is not feasible in the brain, alternative approaches such as X-irradiation have been attempted to induce neuronal loss, for example, in the cerebellum (Altman and Anderson, 1972; Bayer and Altman, 1975).
evidence: This statement explains the technical challenge and references prior approaches.

claim: Loss of Syntaxin-binding protein 1 (Stxbp1) results in massive neurodegeneration.
source: Loss of Syntaxin-binding protein 1 (Stxbp1 – also known as Munc18-1) results in massive neurodegeneration (Verhage et al., 2000), and expression of Cre recombinase in primary cultured neurons from conditional Stxbp1 homozygous mice (Stxbp1fl/fl) induces neuronal death in a cell-autonomous manner (Heeroma et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Expression of Cre recombinase in primary cultured neurons from conditional Stxbp1 homozygous mice induces neuronal death in a cell-autonomous manner.
source: Loss of Syntaxin-binding protein 1 (Stxbp1 – also known as Munc18-1) results in massive neurodegeneration (Verhage et al., 2000), and expression of Cre recombinase in primary cultured neurons from conditional Stxbp1 homozygous mice (Stxbp1fl/fl) induces neuronal death in a cell-autonomous manner (Heeroma et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior study.

claim: Cre recombinase expression under Pcp2 and Sert promoters results in degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells and serotonin neurons, respectively.
source: Moreover, Cre recombinase expression under Pcp2 and Sert promoters results in degeneration of cerebellar Purkinje cells (PCs) and serotonin (5-HT) neurons, respectively (Dudok et al., 2011; Heeroma et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The cerebellum consists of the molecular layer (ML), the Purkinje cell layer (PCL), the granular layer (GL), and deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) in the white matter.
source: The cerebellum consists of the molecular layer (ML), the Purkinje cell layer (PCL), the granular layer (GL), and deep cerebellar nuclei (DCN) in the white matter (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Granule cells in the GL form excitatory glutamatergic synapses with PCs and molecular layer interneurons in the ML.
source: Granule cells (GCs) in the GL form excitatory glutamatergic synapses with PCs and molecular layer interneurons (MLIs) in the ML.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry.

claim: MLIs form inhibitory GABAergic synapses with PCs.
source: MLIs form inhibitory GABAergic synapses with PCs, which then form inhibitory synapses with DCN (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: PCs form inhibitory synapses with DCN.
source: MLIs form inhibitory GABAergic synapses with PCs, which then form inhibitory synapses with DCN (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: ΔGC and ΔPC mice began to show obvious locomotor phenotypes at around P28.
source: ΔGC and ΔPC mice began to show obvious locomotor phenotypes at around P28 (Figure 1B and Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an observation supported by videos and figure showing the phenotype.

claim: Nissl staining demonstrated the loss of GCs in ΔGC mice and PCs in ΔPC mice at 2 months of age.
source: Nissl staining demonstrated the loss of GCs in ΔGC mice and PCs in ΔPC mice at 2 months of age (Figure 1C), but no obvious differences at postnatal days 7–9 (P7–9) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: No obvious differences in cerebellar structure were observed at postnatal days 7-9 (P7-9) in ΔGC and ΔPC mice.
source: Nissl staining demonstrated the loss of GCs in ΔGC mice and PCs in ΔPC mice at 2 months of age (Figure 1C), but no obvious differences at postnatal days 7–9 (P7–9) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The total area of midsagittal cerebellar sections was significantly smaller in ΔGC and ΔPC mice than in control mice.
source: The total area of midsagittal cerebellar sections was significantly smaller in ΔGC and ΔPC mice than in control mice (Figure 1C and D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: In ΔGC mice, the thickness of the GL was reduced by 82%, but the PCL was intact.
source: In ΔGC mice, the thickness of the GL was reduced by 82%, but the PCL was intact.
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from the experimental data.

claim: The PCL disappeared with no change of the GL thickness in ΔPC mice.
source: By contrast, the PCL disappeared with no change of the GL thickness in ΔPC mice.
evidence: This is a quantitative observation from the experimental data.

claim: A significant reduction in the ML thickness was found in both ΔGC and ΔPC mice: 43.4% and 24.9% reduction respectively.
source: We also found a significant reduction in the ML thickness in both mice: 43.4% and 24.9% reduction in ΔGC and ΔPC mice, respectively (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The degrees of ML thickness reduction are comparable to volume fraction of parallel fiber and PC dendrites.
source: The degrees of reduction are comparable to volume fraction of parallel fiber (PF) (Napper and Harvey, 1988) and PC dendrites (Hamodeh et al., 2010; Roth and Häusser, 2001).
evidence: This comparison is made to prior literature measurements.

claim: GCs and PCs were selectively and effectively eliminated in a cell-autonomous manner from the adult ΔGC and ΔPC cerebella.
source: These results indicate that GCs and PCs were selectively and effectively eliminated in a cell-autonomous manner from the adult ΔGC and ΔPC cerebella.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the histological and quantitative data.

claim: GCs project PFs to form excitatory glutamatergic synapses onto PC spines and MLI dendritic shafts.
source: GCs project PFs to form excitatory glutamatergic synapses onto PC spines and MLI dendritic shafts (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar circuitry illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In adult ΔGC mice, PF ablation was confirmed by loss of the PF protein vesicular glutamate transporter (VGluT1) in the ML, except the very surface of the ML and thinned GL.
source: In adult ΔGC mice, PF ablation was confirmed by loss of the PF protein vesicular glutamate transporter (VGluT1) (Miyazaki et al., 2003) in the ML, except the very surface of the ML and thinned GL (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Excitatory PF inputs to PCs and MLIs are mostly ablated in adult ΔGC mice.
source: These results indicate that excitatory PF inputs to PCs and MLIs are mostly ablated in adult ΔGC mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the VGluT1 staining data.

claim: GluD2 shows punctate localization in the ML and increased signal intensity in the ΔGC mice.
source: Punctate signals of GluD2 were observed in both control and ΔGC mice with a 26% increase of signal intensity in ΔGC mice (Figure 2B), which is presumably due to condensation of GluD2 puncta in a thinned ML (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The 26% increase of GluD2 signal intensity in ΔGC mice is presumably due to condensation of GluD2 puncta in a thinned ML.
source: Punctate signals of GluD2 were observed in both control and ΔGC mice with a 26% increase of signal intensity in ΔGC mice (Figure 2B), which is presumably due to condensation of GluD2 puncta in a thinned ML (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data.

claim: GluD2 signal was stronger at the surface of the ML where VGluT1-labeled PFs remained.
source: Notably, GluD2 signal was stronger at the surface of the ML (Figure 2B), where VGluT1-labeled PFs remained (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an observation from the immunostaining data in Figures 2A and 2B.

claim: All PC spines were contacted and formed asymmetrical synapses in the control mice.
source: In electron microscopy analysis (Figure 2C), all PC spines were contacted and formed asymmetrical synapses in the control mice (contacted spine), whereas most spines in the ΔGC mice (87.1% ± 1.5%) were free of innervation (free spine) and wrapped by Bergmann glia (BG in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Most spines in the ΔGC mice (87.1% ± 1.5%) were free of innervation and wrapped by Bergmann glia.
source: In electron microscopy analysis (Figure 2C), all PC spines were contacted and formed asymmetrical synapses in the control mice (contacted spine), whereas most spines in the ΔGC mice (87.1% ± 1.5%) were free of innervation (free spine) and wrapped by Bergmann glia (BG in Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: No difference was observed in the spine number between control and ΔGC mice.
source: Surprisingly, no difference was observed in the spine number between control and ΔGC mice (control, 0.45 ± 0.03 and ΔGC, 0.42 ± 0.02 spines per μm of PC dendrite, n = 142 from three mice each).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: Thick postsynaptic density (PSD), which is typical of asymmetrical synapses, was discerned on free spines.
source: Moreover, thick postsynaptic density (PSD), which is typical of asymmetrical synapses, was also discerned on free spines.
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy data.

claim: The immunogold AMPAR particle density in dendritic spines colabeled with PC protein Car8 was similar between contacted spines in control mice and free spines in ΔGC mice.
source: The immunogold AMPAR particle density in dendritic spines colabeled with PC protein Car8 was similar between contacted spines in control mice and free spines in ΔGC mice (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by immunogold electron microscopy data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Uncaging glutamate-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents were undistinguishable in control and ΔGC mice.
source: We found that uncaging glutamate-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents were undistinguishable in control and ΔGC mice (control, 32 ± 3.9 pA, n = 6 from three mice; ΔGC, 30 ± 3.9 pA, n = 7 from four mice; p = 0.8037, unpaired t-test), and these responses were abolished by the AMPAR antagonist NBQX (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: Uncaging glutamate-evoked responses were abolished by the AMPAR antagonist NBQX.
source: We found that uncaging glutamate-evoked excitatory postsynaptic currents were undistinguishable in control and ΔGC mice (control, 32 ± 3.9 pA, n = 6 from three mice; ΔGC, 30 ± 3.9 pA, n = 7 from four mice; p = 0.8037, unpaired t-test), and these responses were abolished by the AMPAR antagonist NBQX (Figure 2G and H).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiology data shown in Figures 2G and 2H.

claim: Postsynaptic structure and AMPAR localization at the PSD are maintained on PC spines in the absence of presynaptic terminals.
source: These results indicate that postsynaptic structure and AMPAR localization at the PSD are maintained on PC spines in the absence of presynaptic terminals (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electron microscopy and electrophysiology data.

claim: PF–MLI synapses are established on the dendritic shaft.
source: Unlike spiny PF–PC synapses, PF–MLI synapses are established on the dendritic shaft.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cerebellar synapse morphology.

claim: ΔGC mice exhibited a 46% reduction in the density of PSD-95 puncta.
source: In immunostaining for PSD-95, which accumulates at the MLI postsynapse (Fukaya and Watanabe, 2000), ΔGC mice exhibited a 46 % reduction in the density of, and a 43 % increase in the size of individual PSD-95 puncta (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: ΔGC mice exhibited a 43% increase in the size of individual PSD-95 puncta.
source: In immunostaining for PSD-95, which accumulates at the MLI postsynapse (Fukaya and Watanabe, 2000), ΔGC mice exhibited a 46 % reduction in the density of, and a 43 % increase in the size of individual PSD-95 puncta (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: All PSDs were observed on the postsynaptic side of axodendritic shaft PF–MLI synapses in control mice.
source: Electron microscopy showed that all PSDs were observed on the postsynaptic side of axodendritic shaft PF–MLI synapses in control mice (Figure 3B, left), while in ΔGC mice the vast majority (85.8% ± 2.2%, n = 6 images from three mice each) was found in both sides of atypical dendrodendritic contacts between MLIs (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In ΔGC mice the vast majority (85.8% ± 2.2%) of PSDs was found in both sides of atypical dendrodendritic contacts between MLIs.
source: Electron microscopy showed that all PSDs were observed on the postsynaptic side of axodendritic shaft PF–MLI synapses in control mice (Figure 3B, left), while in ΔGC mice the vast majority (85.8% ± 2.2%, n = 6 images from three mice each) was found in both sides of atypical dendrodendritic contacts between MLIs (Figure 3B, right).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: No accumulation of synaptic vesicles with around 40 nm in diameter was observed at the dendrodendritic contact site.
source: At this unique contact site, we did not observe accumulation of synaptic vesicles with around 40 nm in diameter (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The cleft width of the dendrodendritic contact in ΔGC mice (30.0 ± 1.0 nm) was wider than that of axodendritic synapse in control mice (15.8 ± 0.5 nm).
source: The cleft width of the dendrodendritic contact in ΔGC mice (30.0 ± 1.0 nm) was wider than that of axodendritic synapse in control mice (15.8 ± 0.5 nm, n = 63–73 from three mice each).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from electron microscopy data.

claim: AMPARs were localized only on the postsynaptic side in control mice.
source: Notably, while AMPARs were localized only on the postsynaptic side in control mice, they were detected on both sides of dendrodendritic contacts and exhibited a twofold increase in ΔGC mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunogold electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: AMPARs were detected on both sides of dendrodendritic contacts and exhibited a twofold increase in ΔGC mice.
source: Notably, while AMPARs were localized only on the postsynaptic side in control mice, they were detected on both sides of dendrodendritic contacts and exhibited a twofold increase in ΔGC mice (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by immunogold electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Presynaptic active zone protein bassoon was localized at the PF–MLI synapses in control mice.
source: Furthermore, presynaptic active zone protein bassoon, which was localized at the PF–MLI synapses in control mice (Figure 3D and E, left), disappeared from dendrodendritic contact in ΔGC mice (right).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and immunogold data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: Bassoon disappeared from dendrodendritic contact in ΔGC mice.
source: Furthermore, presynaptic active zone protein bassoon, which was localized at the PF–MLI synapses in control mice (Figure 3D and E, left), disappeared from dendrodendritic contact in ΔGC mice (right).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining and immunogold data shown in Figures 3D and 3E.

claim: VGluT1 labeling was absent at and around dendrodendritic contact.
source: We also confirmed the lack of VGluT1 labeling at around dendrodendritic contact (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by immunogold data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The loss of presynaptic elements in vivo induces homophilic interaction between excitatory postsynapses on neighboring MLIs and transforms PF–MLI synapse into unique dendrodendritic contact.
source: These results suggest that the loss of presynaptic elements in vivo induces homophilic interaction between excitatory postsynapses on neighboring MLIs and transforms PF–MLI synapse into unique dendrodendritic contact, at which AMPARs continue to localize at the PSD-like specialization, but presynaptic molecules are no longer clustered (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electron microscopy and immunostaining data.

claim: At dendrodendritic contacts, AMPARs continue to localize at the PSD-like specialization, but presynaptic molecules are no longer clustered.
source: These results suggest that the loss of presynaptic elements in vivo induces homophilic interaction between excitatory postsynapses on neighboring MLIs and transforms PF–MLI synapse into unique dendrodendritic contact, at which AMPARs continue to localize at the PSD-like specialization, but presynaptic molecules are no longer clustered (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electron microscopy and immunostaining data.

claim: After presynaptic neuron ablation, AMPAR clustering is maintained at two distinct types of excitatory synapses, both being at the PSD-like specialization on dendritic spines of PCs and on dendritic shafts of MLIs.
source: Therefore, after presynaptic neuron ablation, AMPAR clustering is maintained at two distinct types of excitatory synapses, both being at the PSD-like specialization on dendritic spines of PCs and on dendritic shafts of MLIs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on both PF-PC and PF-MLI synapses.

claim: In ΔPC mice, calbindin-positive PC axon terminals and VIAAT-positive inhibitory terminals were substantially reduced in the DCN.
source: In ΔPC mice, calbindin-positive PC axon terminals and vesicular inhibitory amino acid transporter (VIAAT)-positive inhibitory terminals were substantially reduced in the DCN (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A few VIAAT clusters remained in the DCN of ΔPC mice, which likely originate from local inhibitory DCN neurons, residual 18.9% PCs, or both.
source: A few VIAAT clusters remained in the DCN of ΔPC mice, which likely originate from local inhibitory DCN neurons (Uusisaari and Knöpfel, 2011), residual 18.9 % PCs, or both.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the immunostaining data with reference to prior literature.

claim: In control mice, the GABAARα1 subunit was clustered on somatic membranes of DCN neurons just underneath VIAAT-positive terminals.
source: In control mice, the GABAARα1 subunit was clustered on somatic membranes of DCN neurons just underneath VIAAT-positive terminals (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 4B and 4C.

claim: The number of GABAARα1 puncta was significantly reduced in ΔPC mice.
source: The number of GABAARα1 puncta was significantly reduced in ΔPC mice (Figure 4C and D), corresponding to the reduction in VIAAT puncta (Figure 4D, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figures 4C and 4D.

claim: The reduction in GABAARα1 puncta corresponds to the reduction in VIAAT puncta.
source: The number of GABAARα1 puncta was significantly reduced in ΔPC mice (Figure 4C and D), corresponding to the reduction in VIAAT puncta (Figure 4D, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunostaining data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: On the DCN somata, the remaining GABAARα1 signal was either dispersed weakly along the somatic membrane or accumulated intensely at sites just underneath remaining VIAAT puncta.
source: On the DCN somata, the remaining GABAARα1 signal was either dispersed weakly along the somatic membrane or accumulated intensely at sites just underneath remaining VIAAT puncta (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Presynaptic components are required for the maintenance of inhibitory GABAAR clustering at PC–DCN synapses.
source: These results suggest presynaptic requirement for the maintenance of inhibitory GABAAR clustering at PC–DCN synapses (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunostaining data.

claim: An AAV-based approach was adopted to investigate the role of presynaptic components in inhibitory receptor localization at GABAergic MLI–PC synapses because of lethality of Stxbp1fl/fl mice when crossed with Cre lines for MLI ablation.
source: To further investigate the role of presynaptic components in inhibitory receptor localization at GABAergic MLI–PC synapses, we adopted an adenoassociated virus (AAV)-based approach (Figure 5A), because of lethality of Stxbp1fl/fl mice when crossed with Cre lines (Nos1-Cre and PV-Cre) for MLI ablation.
evidence: This explains the methodological choice due to experimental constraints.

claim: Only the Nos1 promoter showed GFP expression in MLIs locating at lower ML, but not in PCs.
source: Among these constructs, we found that only the Nos1 promoter showed GFP expression in MLIs locating at lower ML, but not in PCs (Figure 5B and C).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figures 5B and 5C.

claim: Mice expressing Nos1 promoter-driven Cre recombinase showed a significant reduction in neuronal elements of lower MLIs or basket cells.
source: By immunostaining for parvalbumin (PV) and VIAAT, mice expressing Nos1 promoter-driven Cre recombinase showed a significant reduction in neuronal elements of lower MLIs or basket cells (ΔMLI), that is, PV-labeled somata in the lower ML VIAAT-labeled presynaptic terminals around PC somata, and PV/VIAAT-labeled pinceau formation at the base of PC somata (Figure 5D–F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 5D-F.

claim: GABAARα1 clusters on PC somata were reduced significantly in ΔMLI, especially at somatic surface devoid of contact with VIAAT-labeled presynaptic terminals.
source: Importantly, GABAARα1 clusters on PC somata were also reduced significantly in ΔMLI, especially at somatic surface devoid of contact with VIAAT-labeled presynaptic terminals (Figure 5E–H).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figures 5E-H.

claim: After presynaptic ablation, GABAAR is declustered at two distinct inhibitory cerebellar synapses.
source: Therefore, after presynaptic ablation, GABAAR is declustered at two distinct inhibitory cerebellar synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on both PC-DCN and MLI-PC synapses.

claim: Knockdown or knockout of GARLH4/LHFPL4 results in a loss of synaptic GABAAR clustering and inhibitory transmission, though GABAARs are retained on the neuronal surface.
source: Knockdown or knockout of GARLH4/LHFPL4 results in a loss of synaptic GABAAR clustering and inhibitory transmission, though GABAARs are retained on the neuronal surface (Davenport et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2018; Yamasaki et al., 2017), similar to what we observed in DCN neurons of ΔPC mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies and comparison to current data.

claim: Neuroligin interacts with presynaptic neurexins.
source: Neuroligin interacts with presynaptic neurexins (Craig and Kang, 2007; Dean and Dresbach, 2006; Südhof, 2008), which are necessary for excitatory or inhibitory transmission (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Neurexins are necessary for excitatory or inhibitory transmission.
source: Neuroligin interacts with presynaptic neurexins (Craig and Kang, 2007; Dean and Dresbach, 2006; Südhof, 2008), which are necessary for excitatory or inhibitory transmission (Chen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: It remains unknown whether ectopic neurexin expression at excitatory terminals can trans-synaptically recruit inhibitory GABARs to postsynaptic sites in the brain.
source: However, it remains unknown whether ectopic neurexin expression at excitatory terminals can trans-synaptically recruit inhibitory GABARs to postsynaptic sites in the brain.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Nrxn3 knockout specifically eliminates inhibitory transmission in the olfactory bulb.
source: We focused on neurexin-3 (Nrxn3) and excitatory climbing fiber (CF–PC synapses), because Nrxn3 knockout specifically eliminates inhibitory transmission in the olfactory bulb (Aoto et al., 2015), and also because the inferior olivary nucleus (ION) projecting CFs are located distantly from PCs and this provides experimental advantage to avoid potential contamination of AAVs into PCs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: The inferior olivary nucleus projecting CFs are located distantly from PCs, which provides experimental advantage to avoid potential contamination of AAVs into PCs.
source: We focused on neurexin-3 (Nrxn3) and excitatory climbing fiber (CF–PC synapses), because Nrxn3 knockout specifically eliminates inhibitory transmission in the olfactory bulb (Aoto et al., 2015), and also because the inferior olivary nucleus (ION) projecting CFs are located distantly from PCs and this provides experimental advantage to avoid potential contamination of AAVs into PCs (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental design rationale.

claim: The extracellular domain of Nrxn2β fused with the Fc domain of human immunoglobulin interacts with GABAARs.
source: The extracellular domain of Nrxn2β fused with the Fc domain of human immunoglobulin is shown to interact with GABAARs (Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Nrxn3α-Fc pulled down NL2, GABAARγ2 subunits, and GARLH4, but not GluA1 AMPAR, from adult mouse cerebellar lysate, in a calcium-dependent manner.
source: We found that Nrxn3α-Fc pulled down NL2, GABAARγ2 subunits, and GARLH4, but not GluA1 AMPAR, from adult mouse cerebellar lysate, in a calcium-dependent manner (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by biochemical pull-down data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Both GFP and Nrxn3α-GFP are colocalized with presynaptic VGluT2 along CF arbors.
source: Both GFP and Nrxn3α-GFP (green) are colocalized with presynaptic VGluT2 (red) along CF arbors.
evidence: This is an observation from imaging data.

claim: No significant difference was found between AAV-GFP and AAV-Nrxn3α GFP in the number of GFP-positive varicosities per 10 μm axon of labeled CFs.
source: No significant difference is found between AAV-GFP and AAV-Nrxn3α GFP in the number of GFP-positive varicosities per 10 μm axon of labeled CFs (N/10 μm) (n = 34–50 images from three GFP- and Nrxn3α GFP-injected mice).
evidence: This is a quantitative measurement from imaging data.

claim: GABAAR clustering at CF–PC synapses is frequently detected after transfection of AAV-Nrxn3α GFP.
source: GABAAR clustering at CF–PC synapses is frequently detected after transfection of AAV-Nrxn3α GFP, as shown by triple immunofluorescence for Car8 (blue), GFP (green), and GABAARα1 (red).
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining data.

claim: The area and number of overlapped regions between GFP and GABAARα1 per single CF varicosity were significantly higher in animals injected with Nrxn3α-GFP than in those receiving the vector with GFP alone.
source: The area and number of varicosities with overlapping GFP and GABAARα1 signals were significantly higher in animals injected with Nrxn3α-GFP than in those receiving the vector with GFP alone (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative imaging data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Ectopic expression of Nrxn3α-GFP in excitatory presynaptic CFs can trans-synaptically recruit inhibitory GABAARs to postsynapses on PCs.
source: These results indicate that ectopic expression of Nrxn3α-GFP in excitatory presynaptic CFs can trans-synaptically recruit inhibitory GABAARs to postsynapses on PCs (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the imaging data.

claim: Distinct presynaptic dependency of postsynaptic receptors exists at excitatory and inhibitory synapses in vivo.
source: We have identified distinct presynaptic dependency of postsynaptic receptors at excitatory and inhibitory synapses in vivo.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Excitatory AMPARs can localize to PSDs in the absence of presynaptic terminals.
source: Specifically, we found that while excitatory AMPARs can localize to PSDs in the absence of presynaptic terminals, inhibitory GABAARs require inhibitory presynaptic components for postsynaptic clustering.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Inhibitory GABAARs require inhibitory presynaptic components for postsynaptic clustering.
source: Specifically, we found that while excitatory AMPARs can localize to PSDs in the absence of presynaptic terminals, inhibitory GABAARs require inhibitory presynaptic components for postsynaptic clustering.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Fundamentally dissimilar machineries maintain different classes of postsynaptic receptors in the mature brain.
source: Altogether, our findings reveal that fundamentally dissimilar machineries maintain different classes of postsynaptic receptors in the mature brain.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study.

claim: Stxbp1 deletion in 5-HT neurons results in early postnatal lethality.
source: Stxbp1 deletion in 5-HT neurons results in early postnatal lethality (Dudok et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Neonatal or early postnatal lethality was found in Stxbp1fl/fl mice with various Cre lines, including Emx1-Cre, CaMKII-Cre, Nos1-Cre, Grm2-Cre, Grik4-Cre, and PV-Cre.
source: Consistent with this observation, we found neonatal or early postnatal lethality of Stxbp1fl/fl mice with various Cre lines, including Emx1-Cre, CaMKII-Cre, Nos1-Cre, Grm2-Cre, Grik4-Cre, and PV-Cre.
evidence: This is an observation from the current study.

claim: The lethality of Stxbp1fl/fl mice with various Cre lines precluded the use of these mice in studies of mature synapses.
source: This lethality precluded the use of these mice in studies of mature synapses.
evidence: This is an explanation of the experimental constraint.

claim: By combining the Stxbp1fl/fl mouse with the AAV approach, the elimination of specific neurons subtypes can be achieved to evaluate the roles of those neurons on synaptic maintenance, protein function, and behavior, as well as the specificity of Cre recombinase expression.
source: By combining the Stxbp1fl/fl mouse with the AAV approach, the elimination of specific neurons subtypes can be achieved to evaluate the roles of those neurons on synaptic maintenance, protein function, and behavior, as well as the specificity of Cre recombinase expression.
evidence: This is a statement about the utility of the methodological approach.

claim: The overall organization and integrity of the cerebellum remained remarkably intact despite being reduced by >50% in size and the almost complete removal of specific cell populations.
source: Using this highly selective approach, the overall organization and integrity of the cerebellum remained remarkably intact (Figure 1), despite being reduced by >50% in size and the almost complete removal of specific cell populations.
evidence: This is an observation from the histological data.

claim: The brain's capacity to remove cell debris and maintain integrity of the remaining network likely copes with massive cell loss without triggering generalized degenerative responses.
source: Thus, the brain's capacity to remove cell debris and maintain integrity of the remaining network likely copes with such massive cell loss without triggering generalized degenerative responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed data.

claim: Previous studies proposed that networks of cytosolic, transmembrane, and secreted proteins keep neurotransmitter receptors at postsynaptic sites.
source: Previous studies proposed that networks of cytosolic, transmembrane, and secreted proteins keep neurotransmitter receptors at postsynaptic sites (Barrera-Ocampo and Chater, 2013; Gerrow and El-Husseini, 2007; Luscher et al., 2011; Martenson and Tomita, 2015; Moss and Smart, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Presynaptic terminals are required to retain postsynaptic GABAARs but not AMPARs.
source: Surprisingly, our results indicate that presynaptic terminals are required to retain postsynaptic GABAARs but not AMPARs (Figures 2—5), indicating that presynaptic protein, presumably a secreted or transmembrane protein(s), is required to maintain GABAARs at inhibitory synapses, whereas AMPARs require some postsynaptic protein(s), presumably, cytosolic or transmembrane protein(s), for maintenance at excitatory synapses, such as PSD-95-like MAGUK family proteins among others (Garner et al., 2000; Kim and Sheng, 2004).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Presynaptic protein, presumably a secreted or transmembrane protein(s), is required to maintain GABAARs at inhibitory synapses.
source: Surprisingly, our results indicate that presynaptic terminals are required to retain postsynaptic GABAARs but not AMPARs (Figures 2—5), indicating that presynaptic protein, presumably a secreted or transmembrane protein(s), is required to maintain GABAARs at inhibitory synapses, whereas AMPARs require some postsynaptic protein(s), presumably, cytosolic or transmembrane protein(s), for maintenance at excitatory synapses, such as PSD-95-like MAGUK family proteins among others (Garner et al., 2000; Kim and Sheng, 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with speculation about the molecular mechanism.

claim: AMPARs require some postsynaptic protein(s), presumably cytosolic or transmembrane protein(s), for maintenance at excitatory synapses, such as PSD-95-like MAGUK family proteins.
source: Surprisingly, our results indicate that presynaptic terminals are required to retain postsynaptic GABAARs but not AMPARs (Figures 2—5), indicating that presynaptic protein, presumably a secreted or transmembrane protein(s), is required to maintain GABAARs at inhibitory synapses, whereas AMPARs require some postsynaptic protein(s), presumably, cytosolic or transmembrane protein(s), for maintenance at excitatory synapses, such as PSD-95-like MAGUK family proteins among others (Garner et al., 2000; Kim and Sheng, 2004).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the data with speculation about the molecular mechanism and reference to prior literature.

claim: Presynaptic proteins, including Nrxn and Punctin/Madd-4, can induce or specify inhibitory synapses.
source: Also, presynaptic proteins, including Nrxn and Punctin/Madd-4, can induce or specify inhibitory synapses (Graf et al., 2004; Maro et al., 2015; Pinan-Lucarré et al., 2014), which is consistent with our finding that expression of Nrxn3α by excitatory presynaptic neurons recruited GABAARs to postsynaptic sites (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and is consistent with current findings.

claim: Not all CF terminals expressing neurexin colocalized with GABAARs on PCs.
source: However, not all CF terminals expressing neurexin colocalized with GABAARs on PCs (Figure 6), and this appeared to be independent of the expression level of Nrxn3α.
evidence: This is an observation from the imaging data.

claim: The incomplete colocalization of neurexin-expressing CF terminals with GABAARs appeared to be independent of the expression level of Nrxn3α.
source: However, not all CF terminals expressing neurexin colocalized with GABAARs on PCs (Figure 6), and this appeared to be independent of the expression level of Nrxn3α.
evidence: This is an observation from the data.

claim: The incomplete colocalization could be due to the lack of neurexin at the precise presynaptic nanodomain.
source: This could be due to the lack of neurexin at the precise presynaptic nanodomain, as recent studies propose a relationship between the nanodomain structure of synapses and receptor localization (Biederer et al., 2017; Crosby et al., 2019).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism with reference to prior literature.

claim: Recent studies propose a relationship between the nanodomain structure of synapses and receptor localization.
source: This could be due to the lack of neurexin at the precise presynaptic nanodomain, as recent studies propose a relationship between the nanodomain structure of synapses and receptor localization (Biederer et al., 2017; Crosby et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Excitatory presynaptic proteins have been proposed to be necessary for maintaining AMPARs at synapses.
source: Excitatory presynaptic proteins have been proposed to be necessary for maintaining AMPARs at synapses (Barrera-Ocampo and Chater, 2013; Gerrow and El-Husseini, 2007; Martenson and Tomita, 2015), whereas we show that the presynaptic terminal is not required for maintaining AMPARs at the synapse (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and contrasted with current findings.

claim: The presynaptic terminal is not required for maintaining AMPARs at the synapse.
source: Excitatory presynaptic proteins have been proposed to be necessary for maintaining AMPARs at synapses (Barrera-Ocampo and Chater, 2013; Gerrow and El-Husseini, 2007; Martenson and Tomita, 2015), whereas we show that the presynaptic terminal is not required for maintaining AMPARs at the synapse (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: If proteins are involved in early synaptogenesis, net results from altered synaptogenesis may affect receptor maintenance at postsynaptic sites.
source: (1) Changes in synaptogenesis or AMPAR maintenance at synapses. If proteins are involved in early synaptogenesis, net results from altered synaptogenesis may affect receptor maintenance at postsynaptic sites.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation for discrepancies with prior literature.

claim: In the current study, presynaptic neurons were eliminated during or after synapse establishment.
source: In our study, we eliminated presynaptic neurons during or after synapse establishment (Figure 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental approach.

claim: Electron microscopy and uncaged glutamate responses at single dendritic spines demonstrated no changes in excitatory receptor localization and function.
source: (2) Poor resolution in the analysis of synapses. However, we utilized electron microscopy, a high-resolution cell biological approach, and uncaged glutamate responses at single dendritic spines to demonstrate no changes in excitatory receptor localization and function.
evidence: This is a description of the methods used and the findings.

claim: Trans- and postsynaptic mechanisms for maintenance of AMPARs are conserved between two different types of cerebellar synapses in vivo.
source: (3) Divergent mechanisms for maintenance of AMPARs at different type of synapses. However, we showed that trans- and postsynaptic mechanisms for maintenance of AMPARs are conserved between two different types of cerebellar synapses in vivo.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data on both PF-PC and PF-MLI synapses.

claim: Demonstrating the mechanism for AMPAR maintenance at other excitatory synapses in the brain requires the complete removal of presynaptic or postsynaptic cell type, which is not easy to achieve in most brain areas.
source: Of note, demonstrating this mechanism at other excitatory synapse in the brain requires the complete removal of presynaptic or postsynaptic cell type, which is not easy to achieve in most brain areas.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of extending the findings to other brain regions.

claim: Two unusual types of structures were observed in wild-type neurons after elimination of excitatory inputs onto PCs and MLIs: free spines and dendrodendritic postsynaptic contacts.
source: We were able to eliminate excitatory inputs onto PCs and MLIs in vivo, and we observed two unusual types of structures in wild-type neurons, namely, free spines and dendrodendritic postsynaptic contacts, whereas the structure of spines and the PSD were maintained (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the electron microscopy data.

claim: The structure of spines and the PSD were maintained after elimination of excitatory inputs.
source: We were able to eliminate excitatory inputs onto PCs and MLIs in vivo, and we observed two unusual types of structures in wild-type neurons, namely, free spines and dendrodendritic postsynaptic contacts, whereas the structure of spines and the PSD were maintained (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: This is an observation from the electron microscopy data.

claim: PCs can generate and maintain spines without presynaptic terminals.
source: PCs can generate and maintain spines without presynaptic terminals, but dynamic properties of PC spines might be different without presynapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation of free spines.

claim: Dynamic properties of PC spines might be different without presynapses.
source: PCs can generate and maintain spines without presynaptic terminals, but dynamic properties of PC spines might be different without presynapses.
evidence: This is speculation about potential differences not directly measured.

claim: Cbln1 KO and GluD2 KO mice showed 80% and 60% of free spines, respectively.
source: Remarkably, Cbln1 KO and GluD2 KO mice showed 80% and 60% of free spines, respectively (Hirai et al., 2005; Kurihara et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: It remains unclear why some spines are normal and some spines lost presynaptic terminals in Cbln1 KO and GluD2 KO mice.
source: It remains unclear why some spines are normal, and some spines lost presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Free spines have not been observed in different brain regions, for example, hippocampus.
source: In addition, free spines have not been observed in different brain regions, for example, hippocampus (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004), which may indicate that free spines are unstable in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior literature.

claim: Free spines may be unstable in the hippocampus.
source: In addition, free spines have not been observed in different brain regions, for example, hippocampus (Yuste and Bonhoeffer, 2004), which may indicate that free spines are unstable in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is speculation based on the absence of free spines in hippocampus.

claim: The dendrodendritic contacts formed after elimination of PF input were unique in that AMPARs were localized at both sides of the contact, with the wider 'cleft' resembling an adhesive junction.
source: The elimination of PF input resulted in the formation of MLI dendrodendritic contact sites (Figure 3F). These contacts were unique in that AMPARs were localized at both sides of the contact, with the wider 'cleft' resembling an adhesive junction.
evidence: This is an observation from the electron microscopy data.

claim: It is possible that postsynaptic sites on MLI's dendritic shafts express a protein that can form homophilic interactions, such as between cadherin and SynCAM proteins.
source: It is possible that postsynaptic sites on MLI's dendritic shafts express a protein that can form homophilic interactions, such as between cadherin and SynCAM proteins (Biederer et al., 2002; Gavilondo et al., 1982).
evidence: This is speculation about the molecular mechanism with reference to prior literature.

claim: Homophilic interactions may not occur in the presence of higher affinity pre- and postsynaptic protein interactions at normal synapses.
source: Homophilic interactions may not occur in the presence of higher affinity pre- and postsynaptic protein interactions at normal synapses.
evidence: This is speculation about why homophilic interactions are not normally observed.

claim: Homophilic interactions were rare for free spines on PCs in the ΔGC mice, suggesting differences in the molecular compositions of the PSD between PC spines and MLI dendrites or surrounded cell types.
source: In contrast, such homophilic interactions were rare for free spines on PCs in the ΔGC mice, suggesting differences in the molecular compositions of the PSD between PC spines and MLI dendrites or surrounded cell types.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed differences between PC spines and MLI dendrites.

claim: After PFs were eliminated, the PSDs of PC spines may have been stabilized by Bergmann glia, specialized astrocytes in the cerebellum that enwrap PCs but not MLIs.
source: For example, after PFs were eliminated, the PSDs of PC spines may have been stabilized by Bergmann glia, specialized astrocytes in the cerebellum that enwrap PCs but not MLIs (Lemeky-Johnston and Larramendi, 1968; Špaček, 1985).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism with reference to prior literature on Bergmann glia.

claim: Bergmann glia are specialized astrocytes in the cerebellum that enwrap PCs but not MLIs.
source: For example, after PFs were eliminated, the PSDs of PC spines may have been stabilized by Bergmann glia, specialized astrocytes in the cerebellum that enwrap PCs but not MLIs (Lemeky-Johnston and Larramendi, 1968; Špaček, 1985).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Future identification of molecules necessary to maintain pre- and postsynaptic sites may explain the difference in presynaptic-dependent morphology between spine and shaft synapses.
source: Future identification of molecules necessary to maintain pre- and postsynaptic sites may explain the difference in presynaptic-dependent morphology between spine and shaft synapses.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: ΔGC mice manifest ataxia at 5-6 months of age.
source: Cerebellar GC- and PC-specific conditional Stxbp1 homozygous mice (ΔGC mice and ΔPC mice, respectively) manifest ataxia at 5–6 months of age (see Extended Data Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the phenotypic analysis.

claim: ΔPC mice manifest ataxia at 5-6 months of age.
source: Cerebellar GC- and PC-specific conditional Stxbp1 homozygous mice (ΔGC mice and ΔPC mice, respectively) manifest ataxia at 5–6 months of age (see Extended Data Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an observation from the phenotypic analysis.

claim: Gross histoarchitecture of cerebellum is maintained in ΔGC and ΔPC mice.
source: Note that gross histoarchitecture of cerebellum is maintained in ΔGC and ΔPC mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the histological analysis.

claim: The four layers of the cerebellum (EGL, ML, PCL, and IGL) formed similarly in control, ΔGC mice, and ΔPC mice at early postnatal stage (P7-9).
source: The four layers, namely, the external granular layer (EGL), molecular layer (ML), Purkinje cell layer (PCL), and internal granular layer (IGL) formed similarly in control (A), ΔGC mice (B), and ΔPC mice (C). This suggests normal cerebellar formation at early postnatal stage of cerebellar development.
evidence: This is an observation from the histological analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Normal cerebellar formation occurs at early postnatal stage of cerebellar development in ΔGC and ΔPC mice.
source: The four layers, namely, the external granular layer (EGL), molecular layer (ML), Purkinje cell layer (PCL), and internal granular layer (IGL) formed similarly in control (A), ΔGC mice (B), and ΔPC mice (C). This suggests normal cerebellar formation at early postnatal stage of cerebellar development.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the histological data.

claim: ΔPC mice exhibited mild ataxia and survived at least 6 months without extra care.
source: Pcp2-Cre: Stxbp1fl/fl (ΔPC) mice exhibited mild ataxia and survived at least 6 months without extra care, whereas Gabra6-Cre: Stxbp1fl/fl (ΔGC) mice were unable to stand, requiring food pellets and water to be supplied on the cage floor for survival.
evidence: This is an observation from the phenotypic analysis.

claim: ΔGC mice were unable to stand, requiring food pellets and water to be supplied on the cage floor for survival.
source: Pcp2-Cre: Stxbp1fl/fl (ΔPC) mice exhibited mild ataxia and survived at least 6 months without extra care, whereas Gabra6-Cre: Stxbp1fl/fl (ΔGC) mice were unable to stand, requiring food pellets and water to be supplied on the cage floor for survival.
evidence: This is an observation from the phenotypic analysis.
